recs.name: Hold the first payment to a payee, pending a second approver
recs.short: Hold first payment to a new payee
recs.what: Every payee the attacker set up was brand new. Holding the very first payment to a payee stops that payee being used at all — so the 296 follow-on payments to the same fake payees never happen either. That is why it reaches 100.0% rather than the 55% you would get by merely flagging it.
recs.cost:
This is the most operationally expensive of the five. It would hold 2,458 legitimate payments over 90 days — about 27 a day across all 110 customers, roughly one every four days per customer. Every one of those needs a human to approve it, and every one delays a real supplier getting paid. On an accounts-payable platform that friction lands on the customer, not on FinFlow, which makes it the hardest of the five to sell.

A cheaper version — hold only when the payee is new and its bank details are new — cuts that to 686 holds (8 a day, a 4x reduction) and still prevents 91.4% of the loss. That is probably the version worth shipping.

recs.name: Treat repeated failed MFA as a break-in, not a nuisance
recs.what: Three failed challenges for one account inside an hour stops the account. The attacker sent 21 in 51 minutes against one admin and nothing happened.
recs.cost: Measured, not assumed. Fumbling MFA is completely normal here — 229 of 520 real users have failed at least once, 412 failures in total. But real users fail in ones, not bursts: the worst any legitimate user reaches is 2 failures in an hour, and consecutive failures sit a median of 12 days apart. So at a threshold of 3, 0 legitimate users are locked out; at 2 it would be 2. Separately it misses 22 payments ($251,753) from sessions entered before any burst.

recs.name: When one customer is confirmed breached, block the attacker everywhere
recs.what:
This is not "a device at two customers is suspicious". Once a breach is confirmed you already know the machine is malicious, and the only question left is whether the block covers one customer or all 110. FinFlow scoped it to one.

The figure above deliberately assumes FinFlow was slow. We cannot tell from this data when they found out — there is no timestamp on a dispute or a review anywhere in it. But we can prove they found out eventually: ops marked 165 April payments confirmed_fraud and customers disputed 238. Whatever date that happened, it was before 26 June — and the same two machines walked back in and took $2,520,040 anyway. That is the number here, and it holds no matter when the news arrived.
recs.cost:
Almost nothing. The machine is already known bad before the block is applied, so there is no threshold to get wrong and nobody legitimate to catch. This is not the same as treating any device seen at two customers as suspicious — that would be risky, because outsourced bookkeepers do legitimately work across several customers from one laptop.

Upside if paired with the MFA lockout: blocking within a day of the first fraudulent payment would have saved $5,198,392 (88.7%) rather than $2,520,040. That needs detection FinFlow did not have — which is exactly what the MFA lockout supplies, 102 minutes before the first fraudulent payment at org_0001. Containment is only as fast as detection.

recs.name: Raise recall. The precision is already fine.
recs.what: FinFlow escalates 70.4% correctly but reaches only 44.8% of the fraud. Recall is the number to move: 363 fraudulent payments were never escalated at all, and 231 of June's 275 were never even opened. Queue precision is the mechanism, not the goal — with the number of reviews held fixed, the only way to reach more fraud is for more of what you open to be fraud. June had 652 slots for 275 fraudulent payments, so they all fitted with 377 to spare; the queue simply needed to run at 42.2% instead of 6.7%.
recs.cost:
No extra reviewers, and nothing asked of them — they already get the calls right. Of the 78 June payments they escalated, 42 really were fraud (53.8%), and of the 453 they cleared, 0 were fraud.

The honest trade: pushing recall up will push reviewer precision down, because the payments you add to the queue are by definition the less obvious ones. Worth making here — recall fell from 77% in April to 16% on the same attacker in June, and April's number only came after a customer phoned in. The queue works when it is told where to look; it needs to work when nobody calls.

ladder.rule: Any first payment to a payee
